claim: Schizophyllum commune is the most polymorphic species known.
source: Here, we study such patterns in a fungus Schizophyllum commune, the most polymorphic species known.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a factual assertion about S. commune's status among known species.

claim: In S. commune, short-range linkage disequilibrium (LD) caused by attraction of minor alleles is higher between pairs of nonsynonymous than of synonymous variants throughout the genome.
source: Throughout the genome, short-range linkage disequilibrium (LD) caused by attraction of minor alleles is higher between pairs of nonsynonymous than of synonymous variants.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The excess of LDnonsyn over LDsyn is especially pronounced for pairs of sites located within the same gene.
source: This effect is especially pronounced for pairs of sites that are located within the same gene, especially if a large fraction of the gene is covered by haploblocks, genome segments where the gene pool consists of two highly divergent haplotypes, which is a signature of balancing selection.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 1 showing within-gene vs between-gene comparisons.

claim: Haploblocks are genome segments where the gene pool consists of two highly divergent haplotypes, which is a signature of balancing selection.
source: This effect is especially pronounced for pairs of sites that are located within the same gene, especially if a large fraction of the gene is covered by haploblocks, genome segments where the gene pool consists of two highly divergent haplotypes, which is a signature of balancing selection.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about haploblocks and their interpretation, drawing on established knowledge about balancing selection.

claim: Haploblocks are usually shorter than 1000 nucleotides.
source: Haploblocks are usually shorter than 1000 nucleotides, and collectively cover about 10% of the S. commune genome.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Haploblocks collectively cover about 10% of the S. commune genome.
source: Haploblocks are usually shorter than 1000 nucleotides, and collectively cover about 10% of the S. commune genome.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by quantitative analysis in the Results section.

claim: LD tends to be substantially higher for pairs of nonsynonymous variants encoding amino acids that interact within the protein.
source: LD tends to be substantially higher for pairs of nonsynonymous variants encoding amino acids that interact within the protein.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2 showing elevated LD for physically interacting sites.

claim: There is a substantial correlation between LDs at the same pairs of nonsynonymous mutations in the USA and the Russian populations.
source: There is a substantial correlation between LDs at the same pairs of nonsynonymous mutations in the USA and the Russian populations.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: Selection in S. commune involves positive epistasis due to compensatory interactions between nonsynonymous alleles.
source: These patterns indicate that selection in S. commune involves positive epistasis due to compensatory interactions between nonsynonymous alleles.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the observed patterns of LD and supported by inference from the data.

claim: When less polymorphic species are studied, analogous patterns can be detected only through interspecific comparisons.
source: When less polymorphic species are studied, analogous patterns can be detected only through interspecific comparisons.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a comparative claim about detection of epistasis patterns.

claim: Epistasis is pervasive at the scale of between-species differences.
source: Epistasis is pervasive at the scale of between-species differences, where it is saliently manifested by Dobzhansky-Muller incompatibilities and results in low fitness of interspecific hybrids (Callahan et al., 2011; Corbett-Detig et al., 2013; Dobzhansky, 1936; Kondrashov et al., 2002; Orr, 1995; Taverner et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: At the scale of within-population variation, the importance of epistasis remains controversial.
source: By contrast, at the scale of within-population variation, the importance of epistasis remains controversial (Crow, 2010; Hill et al., 2008; Hivert et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Positive epistasis can maintain favorable coadapted combinations of alleles at interacting sites, increasing linkage disequilibrium (LD) between them.
source: In the case of positive epistasis, a situation when a combination of alleles confers higher fitness than that expected from selection acting on these alleles individually, it can maintain favorable coadapted combinations of alleles at interacting sites, increasing linkage disequilibrium (LD) between them (Barton, 2010; Boyrie et al., 2021; Kouyos et al., 2007; Pedruzzi et al., 2018; Takahasi and Tajima, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: In sexual populations, recombination competes with epistasis, disrupting coupling LD.
source: In sexual populations, recombination competes with epistasis, disrupting such coupling LD (Neher and Shraiman, 2009; Pedruzzi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Within a single gene, physical proximity alone may suffice to limit recombination, so sets of coadapted variants may evolve.
source: Nevertheless, within a single gene, physical proximity alone may suffice to limit recombination, so sets of coadapted variants may evolve (Dobzhansky, 1950; Lewontin and Kojima, 1960).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Nucleotide diversity π in S. commune is 0.20 in the USA population.
source: Still, a few hyperpolymorphic species with π>0.1 are known, of which the wood-decaying fungus Schizophyllum commune is the most extreme, where π=0.20 or 0.13 in the USA or the Russian populations, respectively (Baranova et al., 2015; Appendix 3—figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data from prior work and current analysis.

claim: Nucleotide diversity π in S. commune is 0.13 in the Russian population.
source: Still, a few hyperpolymorphic species with π>0.1 are known, of which the wood-decaying fungus Schizophyllum commune is the most extreme, where π=0.20 or 0.13 in the USA or the Russian populations, respectively (Baranova et al., 2015; Appendix 3—figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data from prior work and current analysis.

claim: The two populations of S. commune are highly divergent with dS between populations ≈ 0.34 and Fst = 0.58.
source: The two populations of S. commune are highly divergent (dS between populations ≈ 0.34, Fst = 0.58), but there is essentially no structure within either of them (Appendix 3—figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data analysis.

claim: There is essentially no structure within either the USA or Russian populations of S. commune.
source: The two populations of S. commune are highly divergent (dS between populations ≈ 0.34, Fst = 0.58), but there is essentially no structure within either of them (Appendix 3—figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Appendix 3—figure 2.

claim: In both S. commune populations, at sites with minor allele frequency (MAF) >0.05, LDnonsyn is much higher than LDsyn at the same nucleotide distance.
source: In both S. commune populations, at sites with minor allele frequency (MAF) >0.05, LDnonsyn is much higher than LDsyn at the same nucleotide distance (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The excess of LDnonsyn is much stronger for pairs of SNPs located within the same gene, compared to pairs of SNPs from adjacent genes at the same distance.
source: This excess of LDnonsyn is much stronger for pairs of SNPs located within the same gene, compared to pairs of SNPs from adjacent genes at the same distance.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: The excess of LDnonsyn is independent of whether the two SNPs are located within the same or in different exons of a gene.
source: By contrast, the excess of LDnonsyn is independent of whether the two SNPs are located within the same or in different exons of a gene (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: In S. commune, the recombination rate is higher within exons.
source: In S. commune, the recombination rate is higher within exons (Seplyarskiy et al., 2014), which may affect the patterns of LD; however, this factor could only reduce within-gene LD, and in any case cannot explain the difference between LDnonsyn and LDsyn.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to prior work.

claim: For S. commune, the excess of LDnonsyn over LDsyn holds when explicitly controlling for MAFs.
source: For S. commune, the excess of LDnonsyn over LDsyn holds when we explicitely control for MAFs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), indicating that differences in MAFs between synonymous and nonsynonymous polymorphisms cannot explain the excess of LDnonsyn.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: A much weaker excess of LDnonsyn over LDsyn for MAF >0.05 is also observed in the less genetically diverse D. melanogaster population.
source: A much weaker excess of LDnonsyn over LDsyn for MAF >0.05 is also observed in the less genetically diverse D. melanogaster population (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1B.

claim: In human populations, LDnonsyn is indistinguishable from LDsyn at the same distances.
source: In the still less polymorphic human populations, LDnonsyn is indistinguishable from LDsyn at the same distances (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The excess of LDnonsyn over LDsyn corresponds to the attraction between minor nonsynonymous alleles.
source: The excess of LDnonsyn over LDsyn corresponds to the attraction between minor nonsynonymous alleles.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the observed pattern.

claim: Attraction between minor nonsynonymous alleles can only appear due to positive epistasis between such alleles.
source: This attraction can only appear due to positive epistasis between such alleles - higher-than-expected fitness of their combinations (Appendix 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by theoretical reasoning in Appendix 2.

claim: Positive epistasis can be expected to cause stronger LD in more polymorphic populations.
source: Positive epistasis can be expected to cause stronger LD in more polymorphic populations (Figure 1D–F, Appendix 1) and must be more common for pairs of sites located within the same gene, which are more likely to interact with each other.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by theoretical reasoning in Appendix 1 and illustrated in Figure 1D-F.

claim: For rare SNPs with MAF <0.05 taken alone, LDnonsyn is similar or lower to LDsyn for all three species.
source: For rare SNPs with MAF <0.05 taken alone, LDnonsyn is similar or lower to LDsyn for all three species, consistent with the effects of random drift, Hill-Robertson interference, and/or negative epistasis (Figure 1—figure supplements 4–6; Appendix 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplements 4–6.

claim: Natural selection acting on physically interacting amino acids that are located close to each other within the three-dimensional structure of a protein is characterized by strong epistasis which leads to their coevolution at the level of between-species differences.
source: Natural selection acting on physically interacting amino acids that are located close to each other within the three-dimensional structure of a protein is characterized by strong epistasis which leads to their coevolution at the level of between-species differences (Marks et al., 2011; Ovchinnikov et al., 2014; Sjodt et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Genome-wide elevated LD between amino acid sites within structural domains was recently demonstrated in human populations.
source: Genome-wide elevated LD between amino acid sites within structural domains was recently demonstrated in human populations (Ragsdale, 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In both S. commune populations, pairs of nonsynonymous SNPs are in stronger LD when they are located at codons encoding physically close than distant amino acids.
source: In both S. commune populations, pairs of nonsynonymous SNPs are in stronger LD when they are located at codons encoding physically close than distant amino acids (Figure 2A; permutation test p-value <1e-3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2A with statistical testing.

claim: For pairs of synonymous SNPs, there is no elevated LD when they are located at codons encoding physically close amino acids.
source: This is not the case for pairs of synonymous SNPs (Figure 2A; permutation test p-value = 0.58).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2A with statistical testing.

claim: In the USA population, 8.4% of the genome is occupied by 5,316 haploblocks.
source: In the USA population, 8.4% of the genome is occupied by 5,316 such haploblocks, 56% consist of regions with background LD level, and the rest cannot be analyzed due to poor alignment quality or low SNP density.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and based on quantitative analysis of the data.

claim: Eighty-eight percent of the haploblocks are shorter than 1000 nucleotides.
source: Eighty-eight percent of the haploblocks are shorter than 1000 nucleotides, although the longest haploblocks spread for several thousand nucleotides (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the Russian population, there are 10,694 haploblocks, occupying 15.9% of the genome.
source: In the Russian population, there are 10,694 haploblocks, occupying 15.9% of the genome, and regions of background LD cover 39% of it.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and based on quantitative analysis of the data.

claim: There is only a modest correlation between the USA and Russian haploblocks.
source: There is only a modest correlation between the USA and Russian haploblocks: the probability that a genomic position belongs to a haploblock in both populations is 2.3% instead of the expected 1.3%, indicating their relatively short persistence time in the populations (examples shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative analysis and examples in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: LD within a haploblock is usually so high that most genotypes can be attributed to one of just two distinct haplotypes.
source: LD within a haploblock is usually so high that most genotypes can be attributed to one of just two distinct haplotypes, which carry different sets of alleles (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Polymorphic sites within haploblocks are characterized by higher MAF than that at sites that reside in non-haploblock regions.
source: Polymorphic sites within haploblocks are characterized by higher MAF than that at sites that reside in non-haploblock regions (t-test p-value <2e-16), and in the USA population MAFs within a haploblock are positively correlated with its strength of LD (Figure 3B, Pearson correlation estimate = 0.07, p-value <2e-6).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by statistical testing and data in Figure 3B.

claim: Genes with high LD have the largest excess of LDnonsyn over LDsyn.
source: Genes with high LD, that is those that contain haploblocks, have the largest excess of LDnonsyn over LDsyn (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3C.

claim: LD between alleles of all kinds is higher within genes with large ratios of nonsynonymous and synonymous polymorphisms pn/ps.
source: LD between alleles of all kinds is higher within genes with large ratios of nonsynonymous and synonymous polymorphisms pn/ps (Spearman correlation p-value <2e-16, Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by statistical testing and data in Figure 3D.

claim: Genes with elevated pn/ps have a stronger excess of LDnonsyn over LDsyn.
source: Genes with elevated pn/ps also have a stronger excess of LDnonsyn over LDsyn (Figure 3E, Spearman correlation p-value = 4.4e-17).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by statistical testing and data in Figure 3E.

claim: Positive epistasis alone cannot lead to the observed large excess LDnonsyn over LDsyn.
source: Simulations show that positive epistasis alone cannot lead to the observed large excess LDnonsyn over LDsyn, for which two extra conditions need to be satisfied.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by simulation results.

claim: For a substantial LD between not-too-rare alleles to appear, these alleles must persist in the population for a long enough time.
source: The general reason for this is simple: in order for a substantial LD between not-too-rare alleles to appear, these alleles must persist in the population for a long enough time.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a theoretical explanation.

claim: Positive epistasis must lead to a full compensation of deleterious effects of individual alleles for excess LDnonsyn to occur.
source: First, positive epistasis must lead to a full compensation of deleterious effects of individual alleles.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a necessary condition based on simulation results.

claim: The fitnesses of at least two most-fit genotypes that are present in the population at substantial frequencies must be (nearly) the same for excess LDnonsyn to occur.
source: In other words, the fitnesses of at least two most-fit genotypes that are present in the population at substantial frequencies must be (nearly) the same (Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a necessary condition based on simulation results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: There must be some kind of balancing selection that specifically works to maintain variation for excess LDnonsyn to occur.
source: Second, there must be some kind of balancing selection that specifically works to maintain variation, because otherwise random drift does not allow genetic variation to persist for a long enough time even if some, or even all, genotypes are equally fit (Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a necessary condition based on simulation results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: Balancing selection is necessary for the presence of haploblocks.
source: Balancing selection is also neccessary for the presence of haploblocks, because a pair of divergent haplotypes can evolve in a panmictic population only if they coexist for a considerable time.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a theoretical inference.

claim: The USA and the Russian populations share a large proportion of their SNPs.
source: The USA and the Russian populations share a large proportion of their SNPs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data analysis.

claim: Few shared SNPs between USA and Russian populations are expected to have common origin in the ancestral population.
source: Given the high divergence between the two populations, few such shared SNPs are expected to have common origin in the ancestral population, and instead they are likely to have arisen from recurrent mutation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference based on population divergence.

claim: SNPs comprise 0.28 of all the aligned nucleotide sites in the USA population.
source: The high prevalence of coincident SNPs is not surprising because SNPs comprise 0.28 and 0.13 of all the aligned nucleotide sites in the USA and Russian populations, respectively (Baranova et al., 2015, Appendix 3—figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data from prior work.

claim: SNPs comprise 0.13 of all the aligned nucleotide sites in the Russian population.
source: The high prevalence of coincident SNPs is not surprising because SNPs comprise 0.28 and 0.13 of all the aligned nucleotide sites in the USA and Russian populations, respectively (Baranova et al., 2015, Appendix 3—figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data from prior work.

claim: The values of LD in the two populations are strongly correlated only for pairs of nonsynonymous SNPs located within the same gene.
source: The values of LD in the two populations are strongly correlated only for pairs of nonsynonymous SNPs located within the same gene, and only if both populations carry the same pairs of amino acids in the same sites (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: The correlation of LDs is the strongest if shared SNPs carry the same pairs of nucleotides, but is also observed if they encode the same amino acids by different nucleotides.
source: The correlation of LDs is the strongest if shared SNPs carry the same pairs of nucleotides, but is also observed if they encode the same amino acids by different nucleotides (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The observed pattern of correlated LDs indicates that epistatic selection is shared between the two populations.
source: Thus, the observed pattern indicates that epistatic selection is shared between the two populations.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the observed correlation patterns.

claim: The overall fraction of the genome covered by haploblocks in S. commune is about an order of magnitude higher than the fraction covered by detectable signatures of balancing selection in genomes of other species.
source: The overall fraction of the genome covered by haploblocks is ~10%, which is about an order of magnitude higher than the fraction covered by detectable signatures of balancing selection in genomes of other species (DeGiorgio et al., 2014; Leffler et al., 2013; Rasmussen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by comparison to prior work cited.

claim: Haploblocks in S. commune were shaped by both balancing and epistatic selection.
source: This pattern is much stronger within haploblocks, indicating that they were shaped by both balancing and epistatic selection, so that amino acids common within a haplotype together confer a higher fitness.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the observed patterns.

claim: Haploblocks and positive LD between minor nonsynonymous alleles are common in S. commune due to its hyperpolymorphism.
source: Excessive LDnonsyn in S. commune is also likely to be due to its hyperpolymorphism which increases the probability that mutually compensating alleles at a pair of interacting sites achieve high frequency and encounter each other in the same haplotype before being eliminated by selection.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an explanation for the observed patterns.

claim: In a vast majority of species, π is a small parameter <<1.
source: In a vast majority of species, π is a small parameter <<1.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a general observation about genetic diversity.

claim: Hyperpolymorphic species where π is ~1 provide a unique opportunity to study phenomena which are traditionally viewed as belonging to the domain of macroevolution through data on within-population variation.
source: Thus, hyperpolymorphic species where π is ~1 provide a unique opportunity to study phenomena which are traditionally viewed as belonging to the domain of macroevolution through data on within-population variation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion about the value of studying hyperpolymorphic species.

claim: 34 haploid genotypes from the USA and 21 from Russia were studied.
source: We studied 34 haploid genotypes from the USA and 21 from Russia, each obtained by sequencing and de novo assembly of a haploid culture originated from a single haplospore.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the study design.

claim: The use of haploid samples and de novo assembly of each sample ensures robust identification of haplotypes.
source: The use of haploid samples and de novo assembly of each sample ensures robust identification of haplotypes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a methodological justification.

claim: About 52% of S. commune protein-coding genes had a match amongst the proteins with known structure in the PDB database.
source: Of 16,319 annotated protein-coding genes of S. commune (Ohm et al., 2010) 9,941 were found in all 55 aligned genomes. We blasted the protein sequences of these orthologous groups against the PDB database of protein structures. About 52% of them (5,188) had a match (e-value threshold = 1e-5) amongst the proteins with the known structure.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the analysis.

claim: 22 proteins with significant associations between the patterns of LD and of physical interactions between sites were found in the USA population at 5% FDR.
source: Moreover, it is possible to identify individual proteins with significant associations between the patterns of LD and of physical interactions between sites. At a 5% FDR, we found 22 such proteins in the USA population, and 87 proteins in the Russian population (Appendix 3—table 1); three examples are shown in Figure 2B–D (see also Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Appendix 3—table 1.

claim: 87 proteins with significant associations between the patterns of LD and of physical interactions between sites were found in the Russian population at 5% FDR.
source: Moreover, it is possible to identify individual proteins with significant associations between the patterns of LD and of physical interactions between sites. At a 5% FDR, we found 22 such proteins in the USA population, and 87 proteins in the Russian population (Appendix 3—table 1); three examples are shown in Figure 2B–D (see also Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Appendix 3—table 1.

claim: In a vast majority of species, nucleotide diversity π is of the order of 0.001 (as in Homo sapiens) or 0.01 (as in Drosophila melanogaster) at selectively neutral sites.
source: In a vast majority of species, nucleotide diversity π, the evolutionary distance between a pair of randomly chosen genotypes, is, at selectively neutral sites, of the order of 0.001 (as in Homo sapiens) or 0.01 (as in Drosophila melanogaster) (Leffler et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to prior work.

claim: A few hyperpolymorphic species with π>0.1 are known.
source: Still, a few hyperpolymorphic species with π>0.1 are known, of which the wood-decaying fungus Schizophyllum commune is the most extreme, where π=0.20 or 0.13 in the USA or the Russian populations, respectively (Baranova et al., 2015; Appendix 3—figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Two samples from Florida (USA population) were excluded from the analysis to minimize the possible effect of population structure.
source: Two samples from Florida (USA population) were excluded from the further analysis to minimize the possible effect of population structure.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing data filtering.

claim: The total number of detected SNPs was 5.8 million for the USA population (82% of them biallelic).
source: The total number of detected SNPs was 5.8 million for the USA population (82% of them biallelic) and 2.7 million for the Russian population (93% biallelic).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the data.

claim: The total number of detected SNPs was 2.7 million for the Russian population (93% biallelic).
source: The total number of detected SNPs was 5.8 million for the USA population (82% of them biallelic) and 2.7 million for the Russian population (93% biallelic).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the data.

claim: 25% of the USA SNPs were shared with the Russian population (11% with the same major and minor alleles).
source: 25% of the USA SNPs were shared with the Russian population (11% with the same major and minor alleles), and 53% of the Russian SNPs were shared with the USA population (23% with the same major and minor alleles, Appendix 3—figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the data.

claim: 53% of the Russian SNPs were shared with the USA population (23% with the same major and minor alleles).
source: 25% of the USA SNPs were shared with the Russian population (11% with the same major and minor alleles), and 53% of the Russian SNPs were shared with the USA population (23% with the same major and minor alleles, Appendix 3—figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the data.
